title: How Peyote Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain peyote, the spineless cactus containing the hallucinogen mescaline. They cover its native range in northern Mexico and South Texas, its bitter alkaloid as a defense against animals, its reputation for being hard to find, and its traditional and medicinal uses. The hosts discuss overharvesting by people digging up plants, the 1898-era synthesis of mescaline by Ernst Späth (named as Ernest Smith in the transcript), its effects and long trip length compared with LSD, and the psychedelic-related history involving Aldous Huxley, The Doors, and Alexander Shulgin. They trace peyote's use among the Huichol, the Native American Church and its founding in 1918, Quanah Parker's role in spreading peyote to Oklahoma Territory, the Carlos Castaneda controversy, early Western encounters, the 1890s Parke-Davis peyote tincture, and US legal status including the 1994 religious freedom law and the 1970 Controlled Substances classification. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about eyewitness identification and cross-race recognition.

segments.title: Opening banter and Portland tour date
segments.summary: Hosts open with a Portland, Maine tour announcement, chat about the band Pavement and a Portuguese wine shop, then introduce peyote as an old hallucinogen.

segments.title: What peyote is and where it grows
segments.summary: Peyote is a spineless cactus with a bitter alkaloid, mescaline, that deters desert animals. It grows in northern Mexico and South Texas on rocky limestone, looks like a small bluish-green button with pink, white and yellow flowers, and is hard to spot under nurse plants like creosote and mesquite. Its scientific name is Lophophora williamsii, and it was once confused with other plants.

segments.title: Traditional and medicinal uses of peyote
segments.summary: Indigenous peoples used peyote for religious purposes, indigestion, wounds, energy, and possibly antimicrobial effects. Clinical use in the 1950s for studying schizophrenia was abandoned because results were unreliable.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before discussing mescaline's synthesis.

segments.title: Mescaline synthesis and the psychedelic family
segments.summary: Mescaline was isolated and synthesized around 1918-1919 by Austrian chemist Ernst Späth. It belongs to the phenethylamine family, differing from LSD and psilocybin, which are indoles. Alexander Shulgin's MDMA was inspired by mescaline. Mescaline binds to serotonin receptors, causing nausea and a long trip of about twelve hours.

segments.title: Huxley, The Doors and the word psychedelic
segments.summary: Aldous Huxley's mescaline experience inspired his book The Doors of Perception, which gave The Doors their name, and he coined the term psychedelic after his first trip. Jim Morrison's poetry and albums are discussed.

segments.title: Ancient use, Aztec roots, and Western encounters
segments.summary: Carbon dating of peyote buttons at an archaeological site suggested use back to about 5000 BC (the transcript says fifty BC, which the hosts discuss as seven thousand years). The name peyotl derives from Nahuatl, possibly meaning glistening. Franciscan missionary Bernardino de Sahagún described peyote in the Florentine Codex in the late 1500s. Peyote use later declined under missionary and government pressure to one group, the Huichol.

segments.title: Carlos Castaneda and the Don Juan controversy
segments.summary: Carlos Castaneda, a UCLA anthropology student, popularized peyote among American tourists through books claiming ethnographic study with Don Juan Matus. Scholars have called the books fraudulent, and his companion suggested the character was named after the Portuguese wine Mateus. The hosts compare the controversy to the James Frey memoir case.
topics: James Frey A Million Little Pieces

segments.title: Nineteenth-century Western discovery and Parke-Davis tincture
segments.summary: Dr. J. R. Briggs wrote about peyote's effects in 1887 after a Kiowa man sold him buttons. Parke-Davis of Detroit then sold a peyote tincture. Aleister Crowley reportedly asked for a special batch. Louis Lewin published an early chemical analysis of peyote alkaloids in the late 1800s.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the Native American Church segment.

segments.title: Native American Church, Quanah Parker, and peyote law
segments.summary: The Native American Church spread peyote among many tribes after forced relocation, with roots traced to Comanche chief Quanah Parker, who brought peyote to the Oklahoma Territory after a trip to Mexico. The church was officially formed in 1918, holds ceremonies in tipis for historical reasons, and is Christian-based. Peyote is legal for church members under the American Indian Religious Freedom Act; mescaline was classified as a Schedule I drug under the 1970 Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act. The hosts note peyote is far less potent than LSD.

segments.title: Listener mail on eyewitness testimony and cross-race recognition
segments.summary: A listener living in Japan writes that people are good at recognizing their own race, but this may reflect exposure to people of their own race. Josh responds and the listener offers a Japanese language book by Clayton McKnight.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact info and sign off.
